items.title: UK Supreme Court ruled Uber drivers were workers, not self-employed
items.claim: In February 2021, the UK Supreme Court ruled on the employment status of Uber drivers. What did it decide?

options.text: Drivers were correctly classified as self-employed
Drivers were 'workers' under UK law, entitled to minimum wage, paid holiday and pension auto-enrolment
Drivers were 'employees' with full unfair-dismissal rights
Uber was banned from operating in the UK

items.reveal:
The case ran from a 2016 Employment Tribunal decision to the Supreme Court. Lord Leggatt's judgment held that Uber's contract terms could not displace the reality of control: Uber set fares, terms, the rating system and routes.

Uber subsequently announced UK drivers would be paid minimum wage and pension contributions. The judgment did not give drivers full 'employee' status (no protection against unfair dismissal). Similar litigation has run in California, France and the Netherlands.
items.why: UK employment law has three statuses (employee, worker, self-employed). The 'worker' middle category was created in 1996; gig economy litigation has been the main test of where the line falls.

items.title: Quality assurance and quality control are different things
items.claim: A car plant inspects every vehicle at the end of the line and rejects defective units. Which approach is this?

options.text: Quality assurance, because it ensures quality
Quality control — defect detection after the fact. Quality assurance builds quality into the process so defects don't arise

items.reveal:
W. Edwards Deming, who worked in postwar Japan, argued that inspecting defects out is more expensive than preventing them. His '14 Points' for management (1986) included 'cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality'.

Toyota's andon-cord system stops the line whenever a worker sees a problem — quality is built upstream. Quality control still happens, but as a back-stop, not the main mechanism. ISO 9001 audits processes (assurance), not products (control).
items.why: Two firms with identical defect rates can have very different cost structures depending on whether defects are prevented or caught.

items.title: Most mergers and acquisitions destroy shareholder value
items.claim: Multiple long-run studies of M&A outcomes (KPMG, Bain, Harvard Business Review reviews) report what share of deals fail to create value for the acquiring firm's shareholders?
items.reveal:
KPMG's recurring M&A studies, Bain & Company's analyses, and Roger Martin's 2016 HBR piece 'M&A: The One Thing You Need to Get Right' all converge: 70-90% of acquisitions fail to deliver the anticipated synergies, often because the acquirer overpays.

Specific failures: AOL-Time Warner (2000, $165bn), Daimler-Chrysler (1998), Quaker-Snapple (1994), Microsoft-Nokia (2014). The 'winner's curse' (Thaler, 1988) explains why competitive bidding tends to produce winners who overestimated.

Organic growth tends to deliver more predictable returns but at a slower pace.
items.why: M&A is one of the most-used growth strategies and one of the worst-performing. The gap between expected and actual synergies is systematically positive.
